summary: This unit teaches you to clean the public areas of a hotel or villa property: lobbies, corridors, stairs, lifts, glass, public washrooms and outdoor areas such as terraces and pool decks. You will learn to plan the work, use chemicals and equipment safely, clean in the right order, work around guests politely, and report hazards, lost property and security concerns.

blocks.p: Public areas are the parts of a hotel or villa property that guests, visitors and staff share: the lobby, corridors, stairs, lifts, public washrooms, restaurant entrances, pool deck, terrace and entrance. Guests form their first opinion of a property within minutes of walking in, and that opinion is built largely on what they see, smell and touch in these areas. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees who will work as public area cleaners, room attendants or villa attendants.

Public areas are cleaned while people are using them. That is what makes this work different from cleaning a guest room. You must work **safely, quietly and politely**, with signs out, in a set order, and you must report what you find. Clean, safe public areas protect guests from falls and germs, and protect the property's reputation.

Dilute with a measuring jug, never mix products

Use colour-coded cloths and mops to stop germs spreading

Dust, vacuum, mop and polish in the right order
Clean glass, furniture, stairs, lifts and touch points
Disinfect touch points and refill supplies
Deal with sand, leaves, algae and rain
Keep terraces, steps and pool decks safe and slip-free

Inspect the area as a guest would

flow: Plan and prepare
Put out signs
Collect and litter pick
Dust high to low
Clean glass and touch points
Vacuum, sweep, mop
Check as a guest would
Clean and store equipment

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks, such as cleaning and restocking a public washroom and cleaning a villa entrance, living area and corridor while the assessor and helpers act as guests. The assessor watches your safety, method, teamwork and how you treat guests, not only how clean the area looks.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Team Jamaica (TPDCo) standards and most hotels expect public areas to look clean at every hour of the day, not only after the morning clean. Check your area every time you pass through it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Good cleaners do not just start wiping. They know what must be done, when, and with what. Planning saves time and keeps guests safe.
A **cleaning schedule** is a plan that lists which public areas are cleaned, how often, by whom and by what method. It usually has three levels of work:

head: Level
What it means
Examples
rows: Done every day, often several times
Emptying bins, vacuuming, mopping, wiping touch points, cleaning washrooms
Polishing brass, washing walls, cleaning light fittings, shampooing rugs
A full, detailed clean of one area
Moving furniture, scrubbing grout, cleaning under and behind things

blocks.p: A **checklist** hangs in or near each area. You tick and sign it each time the area is cleaned and checked, so the supervisor can see what was done, when and by whom.

ul: Heavy or noisy work (machine scrubbing, polishing, shampooing rugs, deep cleans) is done when few guests are about: early in the morning or late at night. Fewer people can be disturbed or put at risk.
Light work (spot cleaning, emptying bins, wiping touch points) continues all day.
Busy times, such as check-out in the morning and check-in in the afternoon, are not the time for floor machines or big jobs in the lobby. Clean the lobby edge first, or work one half at a time.
After a spill, a messy delivery or a wet entrance in the rain, clean at once, whatever the time.

flow: Read the schedule and walk through the area
List the tasks and the order
Put on your uniform, closed non-slip shoes and PPE
Collect equipment, cloths, chemicals and signs
Check everything is clean, complete and in good working order
Measure and label the solutions you need

blocks.p: Check each item before you leave the store. Look at the plug and cable of the vacuum cleaner. Look at the mop head. Check the bottles are labelled and not leaking. Check you have enough bin liners, tissue and soap for the washrooms. A missing item means a walk back to the store while guests wait or a spill is left.

blocks.note: Equipment that is faulty must not be used. Switch it off, unplug it, tag it 'Do not use' and report it to your supervisor.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Before you clean, walk through the area as a guest would. Look for spills, litter, damaged items, broken tiles, loose cables, blocked exits, lost property and anything that does not look right. Note them. Deal with the safety items first.

blocks.note: Always start from the cleanest part and the highest part. Dry work comes before wet work. This is the rule for every area in this unit.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Cleaning looks easy, but cleaners are hurt every year in slips, strains, cuts, chemical splashes and electric shocks. In public areas, guests can be hurt too. Know the hazards and the habits that prevent them.

head: PPE
Why you wear it
rows: Prevent slips and protect your feet from spills and dropped items
Protect your skin from chemicals, germs and dirty water
Protect your eyes from splashes when diluting chemicals or cleaning toilets
Keeps chemicals and dirt off your clothes
Used for dusty jobs or strong fumes, as the instructor says

blocks.p: Wear the PPE the label and the task call for. Take gloves off before you touch guests' property, the lift buttons or your face. Change them if they tear.

ul: Put the sign out **before** you start mopping, where people will walk, so it can be seen from both directions.
Keep the sign out until the floor is **completely dry**. Then take it away. A sign left out on a dry floor teaches people to ignore signs.
The usual sign is **yellow**. In a busy lobby, mop one half at a time and leave a dry path.
Wipe up small spills at once. For a big spill, put the sign by it first, then clean.

flow: Look at the load and check the path
Stand close with feet apart
Bend your knees, keep your back straight
Hold the load close to your body
Lift with your legs and turn with your feet
Use a trolley or ask for help if it is heavy

blocks.p: A box of cleaner, a full bucket or a bag of wet laundry can be heavy. Never twist at the waist while holding a load, and never carry more than you can see over.

ul: Check the plug, socket and cable of the vacuum cleaner or floor machine before use.
Jamaica's supply is mainly 110 V, 50 Hz. A cut or exposed cable can cause shock or fire.
Dry hands before you touch a plug or switch. Never use electrical equipment on a wet floor.
Switch off and unplug before emptying a vacuum or changing a part.
Do not run cables across a walkway. If you must, cover them and put a sign out.
A damaged cable: unplug it, tag it, report it. Never repair it with tape.

blocks.h: Sharps, blood, vomit and broken glass

head: Hazard
What to do
rows: Do not touch it with your hands
Use tongs or a sharps kit and put it straight into a sharps box
Keep guests away and put a sign out
Wear gloves and use the spill kit
Absorb, clean, then disinfect the area; bag the waste
Wash your hands and report it
Put a sign out and keep people back
Sweep with a brush and dustpan (do not pick up with bare hands)
Wrap it in thick paper or cardboard and put it in a marked container
Check the floor with a damp paper towel for small pieces
Tie the bag; lift by the neck and hold it away from your body
Do not squeeze or press the bag with your hands (hidden sharps)

blocks.note: If you cut yourself or splash chemical in your eye, tell your supervisor at once. Rinse the eye with plenty of clean running water for at least 15 minutes and get medical help. Fill in the accident record.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Do not stand on chairs, tables or boxes to reach a light fitting or a high shelf. Use an **extension duster** from the floor, or a checked stepladder with someone holding it. Open it fully and make sure it is on a flat, dry floor. Never use a ladder on a wet floor.

Cleaners walk through the whole property and see problems first. Report: broken or loose tiles, loose handrails, blown bulbs, leaks, blocked drains, damaged furniture, broken locks, fire exits that are blocked, fire extinguishers that are missing, and pests. Use a hazard report form (or the property's reporting method) with the **place, what you saw, the time and your name**. If the hazard could hurt someone now, make it safe first: put a cone or sign by it and report it at once. Do not repair things yourself unless it is your job.

blocks.note: Cleaners are the eyes of the property. A hazard you report today may be a fall or fire that never happens.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Cleaning chemicals do the work of removing grease, dirt and germs, but they can burn skin, damage eyes, harm lungs and spoil surfaces. Using them correctly is a skill.

head: Type
Used for
Notes
rows: Mild; safe on most floors; follow the dilution
Spray or damp cloth; do not use on delicate finishes without checking
Often contains ammonia; use with a clean cloth or squeegee
Descaling and cleaning toilets and urinals
Usually acid; use only on toilets; never mix with bleach
Killing germs on touch points and washroom surfaces
Must stay wet for its contact time
Strong disinfectant and stain remover, if the property uses it
Never mixed with other products; diluted as the label says
Can scratch; use only where allowed

blocks.h: Labels and the safety data sheet (SDS)

blocks.p: Every chemical has a **label** and a **safety data sheet (SDS)**. The label gives the product name, hazard symbols, instructions and first aid. The SDS gives full information: dangers, PPE to wear, storage, spills and first aid. Read the label **before every use**. Keep SDS sheets where staff can find them quickly.

head: Label word or symbol
What it tells you
rows: Can burn skin and eyes; wear gloves and eye protection
Can make skin, eyes or lungs sore
Can catch fire; keep away from flames and heat
Can poison if swallowed, breathed or on skin
How long the surface must stay wet with the product for it to work

blocks.p: Many cleaners are sold as **concentrate** (strong). **Dilution** means mixing the concentrate with water to the right strength. Too weak and it will not clean or disinfect. Too strong and it wastes money, can harm skin and surfaces, and may leave a sticky, slippery film.
Always measure with a **measuring jug or a dispenser**, never by eye. Put the water in the bucket first, then add the measured concentrate, to reduce foam and splashes.

blocks.note: A label that says '1 part to 19 parts water' makes 20 parts in all. The cleaner is 1 part out of 20. If the label gives millilitres per litre of water, use that directly. When in doubt, follow the label and ask your supervisor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Label every spray bottle and bucket of diluted chemical with the **product name and the dilution**. Never put chemicals in drink bottles. Someone could drink them.

head: Mixing
Result
rows: Chlorine gas: harms lungs and eyes
Unknown reaction; weaker or dangerous result

blocks.note: Never mix bleach with toilet cleaner, ammonia or any other product. Use one product at a time. Rinse and ventilate between products if the instructions say so. If a gas forms, leave the area, get fresh air and report it.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Store chemicals in their **original labelled containers**, closed, in a **locked store**, low down and apart from food, linen and amenities.
Keep acids and bleach apart.
Return opened bottles to the store. Do not leave chemicals on the trolley in a public area where a child could reach them.
Empty containers: dispose of them as the label says; do not reuse them.
A spill: put a sign out, wear PPE, absorb it (spill kit), clean as the SDS says, and report it.

blocks.note: Chemical splash in eyes: rinse with plenty of clean running water, keep rinsing, and get medical help. Take the label or SDS with the person.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Many hotels use **colour-coded cloths, mops and buckets** so that germs from toilets are not carried to other places. The exact colours vary: always follow the chart the property or the Centre uses. A common system is:

head: Colour
Used for
rows: Other washroom surfaces such as basins and mirrors
General areas such as lobbies, corridors and glass

blocks.p: Never use a cloth from a toilet in any other area. Wash and dry cloths after use, or throw away disposable ones.

head: Item
Use
Care
rows: Sweeping dry dirt, leaves and sand
Removing dust and dirt from carpet and hard floors
Check plug and cable; empty the bag before it is too full; clean filters
Wash, rinse and dry mop heads
Pulling water off glass in clean strokes
Wipe the rubber blade; replace worn blades
Label them; rinse out; do not mix products
Catches dirt and water from shoes at the door
Vacuum or shake out; wash when needed

blocks.p: Use **two buckets**: one holds the cleaning solution, the other holds clean rinse water. After mopping a section, rinse the mop in the rinse bucket and wring it before dipping into the solution again. The dirt stays in the rinse water and the cleaning solution stays clean. Change the water when it is dirty: dirty water only spreads dirt and germs across the floor.

flow: Sweep or vacuum the floor first
Put out wet floor signs
Fill one bucket with solution and one with rinse water
Wring the mop so it is damp, not dripping
Mop in a figure-of-eight pattern, starting at the far side
Rinse and wring the mop in the rinse bucket often
Work back towards the exit and keep a dry path
Leave signs until the floor is dry

ul: **Top to bottom**: dust high things first, so that dust falls onto surfaces you have not yet cleaned.
**Dry before wet**: sweep or vacuum before mopping; dust before wiping.
**Clean to dirty**: start with cleaner areas and end with the dirtiest.
**Far side to the exit**: so you never walk on a floor you have just cleaned.

blocks.p: Use a **damp cloth** (not wet) for dusting. A damp cloth picks up the dust, while a dry duster only pushes dust into the air to settle again. Fold the cloth and use a clean face often. Use furniture polish sparingly and only on wood. Do not spray polish on the floor: it makes it slippery.

ul: Check the plug, cable and the bag or bin.
Vacuum in straight overlapping lines, moving backwards towards the door.
Use the crevice tool for edges, corners and stair edges.
Empty the bag or bin before it is too full, as the maker's instructions say.
Wind the cable loosely; do not pull the plug by the cable.

blocks.p: At the end of a shift: empty and rinse buckets, wash and rinse mop heads and cloths, dry them (damp mops smell and grow germs), clean the vacuum, wipe signs, and store everything in the cupboard in the right place. Report any damage.

flow: Put out signs and collect litter
Empty bins and replace liners
Dust high places with the extension duster
Damp dust furniture, ledges and displays
Clean glass and mirrors
Wipe and disinfect touch points
Vacuum rugs and carpet
Sweep then mop hard floors in halves

ul: Tidy magazines, straighten chairs and wipe tables.
Check plants for dead leaves and water on the floor.
Wipe the reception counter edge where guests lean, but do not move the staff's papers or equipment.
Clean the entrance mat. Rain and mud track in quickly in Jamaican wet weather.
Corridors: litter pick, vacuum, wipe skirting and rails, then mop in halves with a dry path.
Stairs: start at the **top** and work down so you never walk on the clean steps. Check each tread edge and handrail for damage or loose carpet.
Lifts: wipe the buttons, mirror, handrail and door frame; clean the floor; use a sign if needed.
Keep the equipment out of the way of fire exits and never block them.

flow: Wipe the glass with a damp cloth to remove dust
Spray glass cleaner on the cloth, or on the glass if the label says so
Wipe or use the squeegee from top to bottom in straight strokes
Wipe the blade after each stroke
Dry the edges and frame with a clean lint-free cloth
Check for streaks from the guest's side

blocks.p: Do not use too much cleaner. Never use a dirty cloth: it leaves streaks. Clean the lower part of glass doors often because of finger marks.

**Touch points** are the surfaces many hands touch: door handles, lift buttons, stair rails, handrails, light switches, reception counters, pens, remote controls and the flush handles in washrooms. They carry germs from person to person, so they are wiped and **disinfected** more often than other surfaces.

flow: Wipe the surface with detergent to remove dirt
Apply disinfectant and keep it wet for the contact time
Wipe dry with a clean cloth if the label says
Use a fresh cloth or clean the cloth between areas

blocks.p: **Cleaning** removes dirt. **Disinfecting** kills germs. Disinfectant does not work well on dirty surfaces, so clean first.

head: Surface
Method
Avoid
rows: Sweep or vacuum, mop with neutral cleaner
Too much water; wet floor left without a sign
Vacuum slowly in overlapping lines; spot clean stains quickly
Rubbing stains hard; soaking the carpet
Vacuum with a soft tool; spot clean with a damp cloth
Use the product made for the metal

blocks.note: Do not move or touch guests' belongings or staff papers while you clean. Clean around items. If an item is in the way, ask.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Washrooms are the part of the property guests judge hardest. A dirty or empty washroom spoils a good stay.

ul: Knock and call out. Check the washroom is empty.
Put a cleaning sign at the door. Keep the door propped or the sign clear so no one walks in.
Wear gloves, apron and safety glasses. Use red and yellow (or the property's) cloths.
Air the room: open the window or switch on the fan.

flow: Empty bins and remove waste
Apply toilet cleaner under the rim of the toilet and urinal; leave it to work
Clean mirrors, basins, taps and dispensers
Clean the toilets and urinals with the toilet cloths and brush
Disinfect touch points: door handle, taps, flush handle, lock
Refill tissue, soap and paper towels
Mop the floor from the far end to the door
Check, sign the checklist, then clean and store equipment

blocks.p: Work from **cleanest to dirtiest** and top to bottom: mirrors and basins first, toilets and urinals next, floor last. Keep the cloths for toilets apart. Never use them on basins or other places.

ul: Put toilet cleaner **under the rim** and leave it for a short time so that it can work on germs and stains.
Brush under the rim and into the bowl, then flush.
Wipe the seat (both sides), the lid, the cistern, the flush handle and the outside of the bowl with disinfectant, then wipe dry.
Clean the urinal and its drain; check for blockages.
Never mix toilet cleaner with bleach.

head: Supply
Check
rows: Spare roll in every cubicle, holders working
New liners in bins; sanitary bins emptied

blocks.p: Sign the **washroom checklist** each time you clean and check the washroom. It shows when it was last cleaned and checked, and by whom.

blocks.note: A blocked or overflowing toilet: close the washroom off with a sign, do not use it, and report it to maintenance at once. Do not try to clear a serious blockage yourself.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Villa terraces, steps, entrances and pool decks are public areas too. Jamaica's heat, rain, wind and salt air change how they must be cleaned.

flow: Check for hazards: broken tiles, loose rails, algae, standing water
Sweep up loose sand, leaves and litter first
Empty outdoor bins and wipe outdoor tables and chairs
Scrub stains and algae with the right product and a stiff brush
Rinse with clean water and squeegee the water away
Check drains are clear and keep signs out until dry

blocks.p: Always **sweep first**. If you wash a terrace that is still covered in sand and leaves, you make mud and block drains.

ul: Check for broken tiles, loose rails and slippery patches. Wet tile around a pool is very slippery.
Keep chemicals away from the pool, and do not pour cleaner into pool water.
Wipe chairs, tables and loungers; wipe guest towels' stands.
Do not leave equipment where guests walk. Keep the pool gate closed.
Report a dirty pool or low chemicals to the pool attendant or supervisor.

head: Condition
What it means for cleaning
rows: More mud and water at entrances; use more mats, mop more often, put signs out
Clean in cooler parts of the day; drink water; wear a hat; chemicals dry quickly and leave streaks
Sand and salt blow onto terraces; metal rusts; wipe often and rinse
Clear and secure loose items as the property's plan says; clear drains and check for debris
Damp towels and mops grow mould quickly; dry equipment fully

blocks.note: Drink plenty of water and take breaks in the shade when working outdoors in the heat. Tell your supervisor if you feel dizzy or unwell.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Mongooses, lizards, birds and insects visit open terraces. Do not touch animals, clean up droppings with gloves, and report pests or nests to your supervisor.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Greet** guests with a smile and a polite word. Give way: stop work, step aside and let them pass.
Keep equipment and trolleys to one side; do not leave them blocking a path.
Do not talk loudly or chat with co-workers in front of guests.
If a guest asks a question you can answer, answer it. If you do not know, say 'I will find out for you' and check with the front desk. Do not guess.
If a guest complains, listen, say sorry, put it right if you can and tell your supervisor. Do not argue or make excuses.

head: You notice
What to do
rows: A stranger in a staff-only area
Politely ask if you can help; if unsure, tell security
Do not touch it; keep people back; tell security or your supervisor
Someone trying doors or looking into rooms
Do not confront; report to security at once
A broken lock, window or gate
Report it; keep watch if you can
A fire exit blocked or propped open
Clear it if safe and report it

blocks.note: Do not put yourself in danger. Your job is to notice and report, not to catch anyone.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Do not open or search the item more than necessary
Note where and when you found it
Take it to the supervisor or security
Write it in the lost property log: date, time, place, finder, description
Put it in the lost property store
Return it only to a person who describes it correctly, through the proper channel

blocks.p: Describe items by what you can see (a 'black phone with a cracked screen', a 'yellow metal ring'), not by what you think they are worth. Never keep an item. Money, jewellery and phones are handed in and logged at once.

ul: Tie bags when about two-thirds full; lift by the neck and hold away from your body.
Separate recycling (plastic, glass, paper) as the property's system says.
Wash your hands after handling waste.
Keep the waste area clean: it attracts pests.

flow: Walk round the area as a guest would
Put right anything missed
Remove signs when the floor is dry
Tick and sign the checklist
Clean, dry and store equipment
Report faults and low supplies

ul: I can say what a public area is and read a cleaning schedule.
I can explain why heavy cleaning is done at quiet times.
I can collect and check equipment, chemicals and PPE before I start.
I can use wet floor signs correctly, and lift, use electrical equipment and work at height safely.
I can deal with a used needle, blood, vomit and broken glass safely.
I can read a label and an SDS and explain why chemicals must never be mixed.
I can work out how much concentrate to add to a given amount of water.
I can use colour-coded cloths and mops and explain why.
I can mop with two buckets in a figure-of-eight and say the order of work: top to bottom, dry before wet, cleanest to dirtiest.
I can dust, vacuum, polish and clean glass correctly.
I can clean and disinfect touch points and explain why they need extra attention.
I can clean and restock a public washroom in the right order.
I can clean terraces, steps and pool decks, and allow for Jamaican weather.
I can greet guests, give way and deal politely with questions and complaints.
I can deal with suspicious people, unattended bags and found items.
I can report hazards and faults clearly, then clean and store equipment.

terms: Public area
A part of the property shared by guests, visitors and staff, such as the lobby, corridor and pool deck.
Cleaning schedule
A plan listing what is cleaned, how often and by whom.
PPE
Personal protective equipment: gloves, safety glasses, apron, non-slip shoes.
SDS
Safety data sheet: full safety information on a chemical.
Dilution
Mixing concentrate with water to the strength on the label.
Contact time
How long a disinfectant must stay wet on the surface to kill germs.
Touch point
A surface many hands touch, such as a handle, button or rail.
Barrier mat
An entrance mat that catches dirt and water from shoes.
Squeegee
A tool with a rubber blade for pulling water off glass.
Spill kit
A kit for cleaning up blood, vomit or chemical spills safely.
Sharps box
A strong container for used needles and sharp items.
Lost property log
The record of items found in public areas.

c1.title: A busy lobby in Negril
c1.text: At a beach hotel in Negril, trainee cleaner Dwayne is on the 6:00 a.m. shift. The lobby has a tile floor, two large glass doors, leather sofas and a reception counter. Guests start to check out from 7:00 a.m. It rained overnight, and wet footprints and sand are by the entrance. Dwayne has a cloth, a mop with two buckets, a spray bottle of disinfectant and a vacuum cleaner.

c2.title: The washroom near the restaurant in Mandeville
c2.text: At a guest house in Mandeville, Shanique is cleaning the public washroom beside the restaurant. She has a trolley with red, yellow and blue cloths, a bottle of bleach, a bottle of toilet cleaner and a bottle of glass cleaner. A co-worker, Andre, suggests that she mixes the bleach and toilet cleaner in the bucket so the cleaning is 'twice as strong'. Her checklist is on the back of the door.

c3.title: The terrace of a villa in Montego Bay
c3.text: A villa near Montego Bay has a large tiled terrace and pool deck. After a night of wind and a short shower, the terrace has sand, leaves and a few dead insects. Green algae has grown on the shaded steps, and the tiles by the pool are wet. Guests are due to arrive at noon. Cleaner Marcia has a broom, a hose, a stiff brush and a bucket.

c4.title: Notices and finds in a Kingston hotel
c4.text: At a business hotel in Kingston, cleaner Orville is on duty in the corridors and lobby. During his shift he finds a leather wallet on a sofa, sees a man in a plain shirt walking down a staff-only corridor and trying a door, and notices that a vacuum cleaner in the cupboard has a cut cable with wires showing.

c5.title: Dilution and chemicals at the Centre
c5.text: In the practical session at the training centre, a group of trainees is asked to clean the mock villa's entrance, living area and corridor. The label on the neutral floor cleaner says 'Mix 1 part cleaner with 24 parts water.' The measuring jug is marked in millilitres. The group needs 5 litres of mixed solution for the corridor and 7.5 litres for the living area and entrance, and the assessor will walk through as a guest.

questions.q: When should Dwayne do the deep scrub of the lobby floor?
o: Before the guests start to check out, at around 6:00 a.m.
Between 7:00 and 9:00 a.m., when guests are walking through
At noon, when check-in guests start to arrive
Whenever the reception staff are free to watch him
questions.why: Heavy work is done when fewer guests are about, so fewer people are disturbed or put at risk. Check-out time is the busiest time in a lobby.

questions.q: Dwayne is about to mop the wet entrance. What should he do first?
o: Mop the entrance, then put out the sign when it is wet
Ask a guest to stand by the area until it is mopped
Sweep the sand into a corner and leave it for later
Put out a wet floor sign where guests will walk
questions.why: Put the sign out before mopping so people see the hazard from the start. A sign put out afterwards is too late for the first person to walk over the wet floor.

questions.q: Dwayne's list for the lobby floor includes sweeping the sand, mopping and vacuuming the rug. Which is the best order?
o: Mop the floor, then sweep the sand and vacuum the rug
Mop the floor, then vacuum the rug and sweep the sand
Vacuum the rug and sweep the sand, then mop the floor
Sweep the sand, mop the floor, then vacuum the rug
questions.why: Dry work comes before wet work: dry dirt is removed first so that it does not turn to mud under the mop. Vacuuming after mopping would spread wet dirt onto the rug.

questions.q: Which of these should Dwayne wipe and disinfect most often during the morning?
o: The leather sofas, the plant pots and the artificial flowers
Door handles, lift buttons and the counter edge
The tops of the picture frames and the high ledges
The skirting boards and the underside of the tables
questions.why: Touch points are touched by many hands, so germs spread quickly from them. They need disinfecting more often than surfaces that few people touch.

questions.q: Why should Shanique refuse Andre's suggestion to mix the bleach with the toilet cleaner?
o: Together they can give off a poisonous gas
The mixture would be too thick to pour into the bucket
The mixture would damage the cloths in the trolley
The mixture would not be strong enough to disinfect
questions.why: Bleach mixed with an acid toilet cleaner gives off chlorine gas. Using one product at a time is the rule, however 'strong' a mixture seems.

questions.q: What should Shanique do before she starts to clean the washroom?
o: Fill the bucket and mix up a stronger solution first
Take the bins out and mop the floor before anything else
Open the door wide and start from the toilets
Knock, check it is empty and put a sign out
questions.why: Guests must not walk in while you work, and you must not walk in on a guest. A sign at the door protects privacy and safety.

questions.q: Which cloth should Shanique use to wipe the toilet seat and the flush handle?
o: The blue cloth, which she has been using for glass
The yellow cloth, which she has just used on the basins
The red cloth, kept for toilets and urinals only
Any cloth on the trolley, as long as she rinses it
questions.why: A cloth that has touched a toilet is never used anywhere else. Colour coding stops germs being carried from the toilets to basins, glass and food areas.

questions.q: Shanique is nearly done. What is the correct last step?
o: Hang the cloths on the trolley to dry and leave the checklist blank
Check the area, sign the checklist, store clean equipment
Sign the checklist at the start of her shift for all her washrooms
Leave the room and tell the next cleaner to check it
questions.why: Checking the finished washroom as a guest would, and signing the checklist, shows when it was last cleaned and by whom. Equipment is then cleaned, dried and stored for the next use.

questions.q: What should Marcia do first on the terrace?
o: Sweep up the loose sand and leaves before washing
Hose the terrace down so the sand runs into the drain
Scrub the algae on the steps with the sand still down
Mop the terrace with floor cleaner and leave it to dry
questions.why: Sand and leaves turn to mud when wet and block drains. Sweep first, then wash.

questions.q: The tiles by the pool are wet and slippery. What is the best action?
o: Leave them to dry in the sun and warn guests by word
Spread more water over them to wash the sand away
Pour floor cleaner over them to make them look cleaner
Put out signs and dry or squeegee the area
questions.why: Wet tile around a pool is very slippery. A sign warns guests and drying the area removes the hazard. Extra water or cleaner makes it worse.

questions.q: The green algae on the shaded steps makes them slippery. How should Marcia deal with it?
o: Wipe it with a dry cloth and leave the steps as they are
Cover it with a rug so guests cannot see it
Scrub it off with a brush and cleaner, then rinse
Tell guests to hold the rail and take care on the steps
questions.why: Algae is a slip hazard that must be removed, not hidden. Scrub, rinse and dry the steps, and keep a sign out until they are safe.

questions.q: It is a very hot day and the work goes on until noon. What is the best advice for Marcia?
o: Skip breaks so that she finishes before the guests arrive
Drink water and take short breaks in the shade
Wait until she feels dizzy before taking a rest
Wear a long, heavy coat to protect her from the sun
questions.why: Working in the heat can cause exhaustion and dizziness. Drinking water and resting in the shade protect you, and you should report it if you feel unwell.

questions.q: What should Orville do with the wallet he finds on the sofa?
o: Hand it to his supervisor or security to be logged
Check inside for the owner's name and phone him himself
Leave it on the sofa in case the guest comes back soon
Put it in his locker until the end of his shift
questions.why: All found items are handed in and logged at once so they can be returned to the right owner and nobody is blamed later.

questions.q: Orville sees a man he does not know trying a door in the staff-only corridor. What is the best action?
o: Stand in front of the man and ask him to leave the corridor
Follow him around the hotel until he leaves the building
Ignore it, because the man is not wearing a uniform
Report it to security at once and keep a safe distance
questions.why: Cleaners notice and report. Confronting a stranger can put you at risk, so call security and give a clear description.

questions.q: What should Orville do about the vacuum cleaner with the cut cable?
o: Wrap the cut cable in tape and use it on the dry floors
Use it only on the carpet in the corridor
Unplug it, tag it 'do not use' and report it
Leave it in the cupboard without telling anyone
questions.why: Exposed wires can cause electric shock or fire. Faulty equipment is taken out of use, tagged and reported so that nobody uses it by mistake.

questions.q: A guest stops Orville in the corridor to ask where the airport taxi stand is. He is not sure. What should he say?
o: 'Try the front gate, it is probably there'
'I will find out,' then check with the front desk
'I do not know,' then carry on with the mopping
'Ask someone else,' and walk on down the corridor
questions.why: Never guess: a wrong answer wastes a guest's time. Offering to find out, then asking the front desk, shows courtesy and gives the right information.

questions.q: How much floor cleaner does the group need to make the 5 litres of mixed solution?
o: 200 ml
120 ml
25 ml
1 litre
questions.why: 1 part cleaner + 24 parts water = 25 parts in all. 5000 ml / 25 = 200 ml of cleaner, and the rest is water. Always measure with the jug.

questions.q: How much cleaner is needed for the 7.5 litres of mixed solution?
o: 180 ml
75 ml
750 ml
300 ml
questions.why: 7500 ml / 25 parts = 300 ml. Measure each time rather than guessing, because too weak will not clean and too strong leaves a slippery film.

questions.q: One trainee says the group should add extra cleaner 'because the floor is dirty'. What is the correct reply?
o: Add extra, because it will work faster and better
Add extra, but use cooler water to balance it out
Follow the label, as extra can leave a slippery film
Add extra for the corridor and less for the living area
questions.why: A stronger mix wastes money and can leave a film that holds dirt and makes the floor slippery. Follow the label and use the right method for dirty floors.

questions.q: When the group finishes, what should happen to the mops, cloths and buckets?
o: Left wet in the buckets for the next group to use
Washed, rinsed, dried and stored in the cupboard
Hung up on the trolley in the corridor to dry
Put away as they are, to save time at the end
questions.why: Wet mops and cloths grow germs and smell. Equipment is washed, dried and stored so it is ready and clean for the next use.
